explanation: Modern computer systems employ a memory hierarchy to bridge the speed gap between CPU and main memory.  This hierarchy consists of multiple levels of storage with varying speeds and capacities.  Caches, the fastest level, are small, fast memory units that hold frequently accessed data.  Cache mapping determines how data from main memory is placed into and retrieved from the cache. Understanding cache mapping is crucial for performance optimization because it directly impacts how efficiently the CPU accesses data.
syntax: Cache mapping strategies are generally categorized as direct-mapped, set-associative, and fully associative.  Each has a different method for mapping memory addresses to cache locations. This involves dividing the memory address into tag, set index, and block offset bits.  The number of bits in each field determines the cache size, set associativity, and block size.

example_explanation: This example demonstrates the partitioning of a 32-bit memory address into tag, index, and block offset fields for a direct-mapped cache.  The tag uniquely identifies a block of data in main memory. The index determines which cache set the block resides in (in this case, one of 256 sets).  The block offset indicates the word within the block.  In a direct-mapped cache, a given memory address will always map to the same cache location.  This example highlights how the cache organization affects memory access speed and illustrates the fundamental principles of cache mapping as described in the provided text regarding Figure 6.26 (which shows cache parameters influencing address partitioning).
